newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK GOVERNMENT APPROVES CREATION OF EXIM BANK.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK GOVERNMENT APPROVES CREATION OF EXIM BANK.

text.p: The Slovak government on Tuesday approved the creation of an export-import bank, designed to boost exports and curb a burgeoning trade deficit.

"The idea of an Ex-Im bank is based on the need to have an institution providing financial and insurance backing of Slovak export loans, mainly the medium-term and long-term credits," Maria Kovacova, head of the finance ministry economic policy department, told a news conference.

Speaking after a cabinet session which approved the move Kovacova said the bank, to be 100-percent state owned, will start with two billion crowns basic capital taken from the 1997 state budget "sometime in the second quarter of next year".
Slovak exporters are to contribute to the bank's funds with a sum equal to 0.05 percent of their annual turnover.
The law on the creation of the bank is expected to be approved by the parliament by the end of this year, so that it could come into effect on January 1.
"Though we expect the law to be effective from the beginning of next year, the launch of the bank's activities will be a little delayed," Kovacova said.
"(But) we have to prepare the organisation conditions for lauch of the operations by the end of the first quarter, so that it could start in the next few months," she added.
Kovacova said that the bank will support only large export projects approved by the government. The cabinet will be also the only control body over the bank.
"We expect the bank to cover about 30 percent of the Slovak exports, and its balance sum should total some 70 billion crowns when it gets into top gear," Kovacova said.
Slovakia's foreign trade deficit totalled 42.52 billion crowns ($1.37 billion) in the first ten months of this year, up from a 37.17 billion deficit for the January-September period.
This compares with a a trade surplus of 18.79 billion crowns for the first 10 months of 1995.

Government officials have repeatedly said the widening trade gap was not reason for concern, as it caused mainly by imports of technology needed for economic restructuring and row materials, such as natural gas and crude oil. -- Peter Laca, Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-563-3687
